title: Polynomial kernel for Planar Edge Deletion
formal:
Does Planar Edge Deletion admit a deterministic polynomial kernel parameterized by the edge-deletion budget \(k\)?

An instance consists of a finite simple undirected graph \(G\) and an integer \(k\ge0\). Write
\[
\operatorname{PED}(G,k)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists F\subseteq E(G):\ |F|\le k\ \text{and}\ G-F\ \text{is planar}.
\]
Here \(G-F\) retains all vertices and removes exactly the edges in \(F\). There is no promise on the input graph.

Precisely, do there exist one deterministic multitape Turing machine \(M\) and fixed integers \(C,a,b\ge1\) such that, on every valid input of bit length \(L\), \(M\) halts within \(C(L+1)^a\) bit steps and outputs a valid instance \((G',k')\) of this same problem satisfying
\[
\operatorname{PED}(G,k)\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \operatorname{PED}(G',k'),
\qquad
|\operatorname{enc}(G',k')|+k'\le C(k+1)^b?
\]
The program, constants and exponents are independent of \(G\) and \(k\). There is no complexity-theoretic assumption in this existence question.
why: Planar Edge Deletion is a concrete test of whether a graph close to a central minor-closed class can be reduced efficiently to polynomially many relevant bits. A polynomial kernel would bound the information needed for exact edge repair solely by the repair budget, despite an arbitrarily large input graph. Its position between fixed-parameter algorithms, graph-minor structure and the broader forbidden-minor edge-deletion question gives it significance beyond one reduction rule.
status_note: Explicitly open as an edge-deletion polynomial-kernel question in arXiv version 2 from 2020 and in the published survey from 26 April 2023. The status records a sourced open problem with that review limit; it is not an exhaustive literature certificate or a claim of completed Lean verification.

importance.reason: A core graph-preprocessing question for exact edge repair to planarity, explicitly retained as a separate open case in the edge-modification survey. Its importance comes from the gap between known fixed-parameter solvability and polynomial preprocessing, and from its role as a concrete nontrivial case of forbidden-minor edge deletion. sentences: Planar Edge Deletion asks whether at most k edges can be removed from an arbitrary graph to make it planar.
The question is whether deterministic polynomial-time preprocessing always produces one equivalent instance whose total size is polynomial in k.
Both the deletion budget and the complete output encoding are bounded, with no randomness, approximation or oracle queries.
Fixed-parameter algorithms and approximate vertex-deletion kernels have different guarantees and do not settle this exact edge problem.
A complete Lean answer must establish such a uniform kernel or prove that every deterministic polynomial-time exact preprocessor fails a polynomial size bound.

definitions:
A finite simple undirected graph on \(n\ge0\) labelled vertices has vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and an edge set consisting of unordered pairs of distinct vertices. There are no loops, parallel edges, weights, protected edges or terminal sets. Disconnected graphs and isolated vertices are allowed. The empty graph is planar.

A graph is planar if it admits a drawing in \(\mathbb R^2\) that assigns distinct points to vertices and represents every edge by an injective continuous arc joining its endpoints, such that no edge interior contains a vertex point and two edge arcs intersect only at their common endpoints. An embedding is not supplied as part of the input. Every edge has unit deletion cost. The budget counts deleted edges, not deleted vertices, contractions, crossing points or a change to an existing drawing.

Fix the following binary encoding. For a nonnegative integer \(t\), let \(\operatorname{bin}(t)\) be its ordinary binary expansion without leading zeros, with \(\operatorname{bin}(0)=0\), and let \(\ell(t)\) be its length. Encode \(t\) as \(1^{\ell(t)}0\operatorname{bin}(t)\). Encode \((G,k)\) as the concatenation of this integer encoding of \(n\), the \(\binom n2\) adjacency bits in lexicographic order of pairs \(1\le i<j\le n\), and the integer encoding of \(k\). An adjacency bit is one exactly when the corresponding edge belongs to \(E(G)\). The total number of bits is \(L=|\operatorname{enc}(G,k)|\). Output instances use the identical convention, with their own labels \([n']\). No behavior on malformed encodings is required.

A deterministic multitape Turing machine has a fixed finite program, a fixed finite alphabet and a fixed finite number of tapes. A transition reads and writes a bounded number of tape symbols and moves each head by at most one cell. Its work tapes start blank; all input access, computation and output writing count toward the time bound. There is no randomization, oracle, nonuniform advice or operation on an unbounded integer at unit cost. The time bound is polynomial in the binary input length, not in the numerical value of an arbitrarily large binary budget.

The kernel outputs a single unweighted graph and a nonnegative integer parameter for Planar Edge Deletion. It preserves the exact yes/no answer on every instance. It need not preserve the optimum deletion number, return a particular deletion set, or make \(k'\le k\); the numerical value \(k'\) must satisfy the displayed polynomial bound. The output graph need not be a subgraph or minor of \(G\), and the kernel may create and relabel graph elements. These preprocessing freedoms do not change the permitted operation in either input or output decision instance, which is edge deletion.

The bound includes the entire output encoding as well as the numerical output budget. A bound on a selected graph parameter alone is insufficient unless the total bound follows from it. All finite input budgets are admitted. In particular, \(k\ge |E(G)|\) gives a yes-instance because deleting every edge leaves a planar graph. The convention \(k+1\) also includes the case \(k=0\).

The required output belongs to the same parameterized problem. A compression to another language, an annotated or weighted instance, several oracle queries, or an approximate decision threshold is not itself such a kernel. A result in one of those formats qualifies only if its complete conversion into the specified single equivalent instance, with the required time and size bounds, is proved.
answer_criterion:
Provide a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of the displayed kernel-existence statement or of its full negation.

For a positive answer, establish one fixed machine and constants \(C,a,b\) with the time, exact equivalence, valid-output and size guarantees for every graph and budget in the stated domain.

The negative statement quantifies over all deterministic polynomial-time preprocessing algorithms that return a valid equivalent Planar Edge Deletion instance on every input. It requires proving that, for every such algorithm \(M\) and all integers \(D,s\ge1\), some input \((G,k)\) has output \((G',k')=M(G,k)\) with
\[
|\operatorname{enc}(G',k')|+k'>D(k+1)^s.
\]
This is equivalent to the full negation of the displayed existence statement; its constants for running time and output size can be combined by increasing a common \(C\).

A failure of one reduction system or one proposed algorithm is not a negative answer. A conditional lower bound does not establish this unconditional negation unless its additional assumptions are also established. A fixed-parameter decision algorithm, a vertex-deletion kernel, a result assuming the input is already planar, or a randomized or approximate kernel must establish the exact statement above to qualify. The target is existence of polynomial preprocessing, not a numerical estimate of the minimum deletion count.

context_blocks.text: The source uses Planar Deletion as shorthand for Planar Edge Deletion and explicitly permits deleting at most k edges. Its Open Problem 2.12 asks for a polynomial kernel in that budget. The present title makes the operation visible so that it cannot be mistaken for deleting vertices.

Fixed-parameter tractability is already known, so the issue is the strength of polynomial-time preprocessing. A fixed-parameter algorithm may spend a large parameter-dependent amount of time deciding an instance, whereas a kernel must run in polynomial input time before producing its smaller equivalent instance. The May 2026 full version of the crossing-number framework gives a direct fixed-parameter result for this edge-deletion problem under the name skewness.

Planarity is characterized by excluding the complete graph on five vertices and the complete bipartite graph with two parts of size three as minors. Consequently, this is a concrete case of the source’s next question about edge deletion to exclude any fixed finite forbidden-minor family. A positive answer for this case alone would not establish that broader assertion.

Deleting vertices has different consequences because one deleted vertex removes all its incident edges. General vertex-deletion kernel theorems for forbidden families containing a planar graph do not cover planarization, whose two forbidden minors are both nonplanar. The STACS 2026 discussion explicitly retains exact Planar Vertex Deletion kernelization as open and distinguishes its known approximate kernel.

The published 2023 survey retains the exact edge-deletion kernel question. Later fixed-parameter algorithms and structural or approximate vertex-deletion results checked in this review have different guarantees. They are recorded as context without treating them as either a polynomial kernel or an unconditional obstruction for the present problem.

checked_sources: Read the complete active TCS-7022, docs/RULES.md, and active related cards TCS-4695 and TCS-7023. TCS-4695 concerns vertex deletion for arbitrary fixed forbidden families, and TCS-7023 quantifies over all fixed forbidden families for edge deletion. TCS-7022 is a special case of the latter for {K5,K3,3}, but its individual truth value is not equivalent to that universal assertion. Preserve both relations; no neighboring canonical card was modified.

Downloaded and read the actual arXiv:2001.06867v2 PDF, dated 19 February 2020. Section 1 p. 4 defines polynomial kernels as polynomial-time same-problem reductions whose instance-plus-parameter size is polynomial in k. The pp. 12–13 paragraph explicitly says delete at most k edges to obtain a planar graph; p. 13 Open Problem 2.12 asks whether a polynomial kernel exists. There is no source ambiguity between edge and vertex operations after reading this paragraph.

Downloaded and read the actual published 2023 survey from Fedor Fomin’s author site. Metadata on p. 1 identifies Computer Science Review 48 (2023), 100556, DOI 10.1016/j.cosrev.2023.100556, available online 26 April 2023. Printed p. 8 retains Open Problem 2.12, the edge definition, and the adjacent general edge-deletion question. No claim that the 2020 page number applies to the journal edition.

The deterministic convention is the ordinary unqualified kernel convention; the survey separately labels randomized kernels elsewhere. The original definition permits time polynomial in |I| and numerical k. Requiring time polynomial in binary input length is equivalent for this problem: budgets at least |E(G)| can be recognized as yes and replaced by a fixed yes-instance, while remaining budgets are polynomially bounded in the explicitly encoded graph size. The k+1 convention covers zero. The source size |I-prime|+k-prime and the card’s total output encoding plus k-prime differ only by polynomially bounded delimiters and parameter encoding.

The dense adjacency-bit representation fixes a non-succinct graph encoding. Standard explicitly listed vertex/edge representations are polynomially interconvertible; no claim of equivalence to succinct encodings with an exponentially large implicit isolated-vertex set. Simple graphs, unit deletion costs and no annotations are the ordinary graph-modification model. The kernel need not retain the original vertices, be a minor, or follow specified local reduction rules.

Read actual arXiv:2410.00206v4, 6 May 2026, Section 5.4 p. 23 and Proposition 5.9. Skewness is exactly the minimum number of edges whose deletion leaves a planar graph. With the sphere fixed, t=0, and one deletion color, the proposition gives a uniform FPT decision algorithm for this card’s problem. Its parameter-dependent factor does not constitute polynomial-time kernelization. The same source says the older Kawarabayashi–Reed and Jansen–Lokshtanov–Saurabh linear FPT algorithms were claimed without details, so the draft uses the checked later proposition rather than claiming to have audited those older proofs.

Downloaded and read STACS 2026 article 17, introductory pp. 17:2–17:3 and Theorem 1. The exact solution-budget kernel for Planar Vertex Deletion remains open there; the known planarization result is approximate. The source’s planar-family vertex theorem assumes the forbidden family contains a planar graph, which {K5,K3,3} does not. Neither result settles this edge-deletion task.

Bounded searches through 16 September 2026 checked the exact names Planar Edge Deletion, Edge Planarization, Planar Deletion, skewness and polynomial kernel. No exact polynomial kernel or unconditional nonexistence theorem was recovered. Search results for Edge Multiway Cut on planar inputs, outerplanar vertex deletion, crossing-number variants and vertex explosion concern different problems.

A secondary search result led to Bart Jansen’s 2026 Quo Vadis, Kernelization? DOI 10.1016/j.cosrev.2026.101035. Publisher/Crossref metadata are available (November 2026 issue, a July 2026 license date), but the attempted public full-text routes returned metadata only or HTTP 403. The asserted Edge Planarization passage was not recovered from the primary full text, so it is not used as a checked current-open-status citation or included in public references. The cached XML and short text for that lead contain metadata only, not the article.

No conditional complexity hypothesis is added. The source asks existence of a polynomial kernel. Its literal negative answer is unconditional; an implication from a kernel to NP contained in coNP/poly remains conditional evidence unless the necessary separation assumption is proved. The public criterion states this distinction without replacing the source question by a conditional one.
